rewritten_text:
Her position was unusually painful and difficult. She longed intensely to uncover the mystery surrounding Oliver's past. Yet she also felt bound to protect the secret that the unhappy woman she had just spoken with had entrusted to her, a young and innocent girl. The woman's words and manner had touched Rose Maylie deeply. Alongside her love for the boy in her care, and almost as strong and sincere, was her desire to help this outcast find repentance and hope.

They intended to stay in London for only three days before spending several weeks on a distant stretch of coast. It was already midnight on the first day. What could Rose decide to do that could be accomplished within forty-eight hours? And how could she delay their departure without raising suspicions?

Mr. Losberne was staying with them and would remain for the next two days. But Rose knew the good gentleman's impulsive temper too well. She could easily imagine his first furious reaction toward the person who had helped recapture Oliver. She dared not tell him the secret when she had no experienced person beside her to support her appeal on the girl's behalf. For the same reasons, she would need to be extremely careful in telling Mrs. Maylie, whose first response would certainly be to consult the worthy doctor. Even if Rose had known how to contact a lawyer, she could hardly consider it for that same reason. Once she thought of asking Harry for help. But this reminded her of their last parting. It seemed unfair to call him back when perhaps—tears filled her eyes as she considered it—he had already learned to forget her and was happier away.

These conflicting thoughts kept Rose awake and anxious all night. She leaned toward one plan, then another, then rejected them all as fresh difficulties came to mind. After further thought the next day, she finally decided, in desperation, to consult Harry.

‘If coming back here hurts him,’ she thought, ‘how much it will hurt me! But perhaps he won't come. He may write, or he may come himself and take care to avoid seeing me, as he did when he went away. I hardly expected him to do that, but it was better for both of us.’ At this, Rose let her pen fall and turned aside, as though even the sheet of paper that would carry her message must not be allowed to see her cry.

My heart was pounding, and I felt afraid without knowing why. I sent the servant away, locked my door, and sat down to read my father's letter. This is what it said.

‘My dear child,

‘I have betrayed your trust. I have tried to corrupt your mind and exposed your innocent heart to the looks and language of a forbidden, monstrous passion. I must pay for these crimes, and try to make my punishment fit my guilt. I have no doubt you are prepared for what I must tell you: we must part and remain apart forever.

‘I am taking away your parent and your only friend. You are left without protection in the world. Your hopes are shattered; the peace and safety of your pure mind are destroyed. Memory will bring you terrible pictures of guilt and the pain of innocent love betrayed. Yet I, who cause all this suffering, who cast you out and have mercilessly marked my own child's heart and face with distrust and agony, beg you to forgive me in the overflowing anguish of my heart. With devilish carelessness I have tried to steal away your beauty and put the ugly deformity of sin in its place.

‘I do not ask for pity. You must hate me, and you do. But forgive me, Mathilda; do not follow me into exile with thoughts of unforgiving anger. I must never see you or hear your voice again. Yet the gentle whisper of your forgiveness will reach me and cool my fevered mind and heart. I am certain I would feel it even in my grave. I dare to strengthen this plea by telling you how unhappily I was caught in this net of burning torment, and how I struggled to escape it. If your soul were less pure and bright, I would not try to defend myself before you. I would fear that, by making you hate me less, I might also make you hate wrongdoing less. But speaking to you feels like appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness. I must try to gain it, or give up all hope. So I beg you to hear me. If good people believe that terrible suffering and remorse that tears at the mind like madness can lessen guilt at all, perhaps you may think—though I dare not—that I deserve some compassion from you.

‘Please remember our first happy life together beside Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen years of exhausting travel. Through all the dangers and misfortunes of those years, my heart had remained completely empty of affection.’

‘Yes, it is—and I could have got it myself if I'd been big enough. I spotted him first. Who caught him?’

‘Some old fellow, a stranger. He sold his claim for forty dollars because he has to go upriver and can't wait. Just think of that! You can bet I'd wait, even if it took seven years.’

‘So would I, every time,’ I said. ‘But maybe his claim isn't worth any more than that, if he's willing to sell so cheap. Maybe something about it isn't right.’

‘It's right, all right—as straight as can be. I saw the notice myself. It describes him exactly, like a picture, and names the plantation he comes from, below New Orleans. No sir, there's nothing doubtful about that bargain, you can count on it. Say, could you give me a chew of tobacco?’

I didn't have any, so he went away. I returned to the raft and sat in the shelter to think. But I couldn't work anything out. I thought until my head hurt and still couldn't find a way out of the trouble. After such a long journey, after everything we'd done for those scoundrels, it had all come to nothing. Everything was wrecked because they could bring themselves to play that trick on Jim, to make him a slave again for the rest of his life, among strangers too, for forty lousy dollars.

At one point I told myself that, if Jim had to be a slave, it would be a thousand times better for him to be back home with his family. So perhaps I should write to Tom Sawyer and ask him to tell Miss Watson where Jim was. But I soon dropped that idea for two reasons. She would be furious and disgusted at his wickedness and ingratitude in leaving her, and would sell him straight down the river again. And even if she didn't, everyone naturally despised an ungrateful Black man. They would remind Jim of it constantly, making him feel worthless and disgraced. Then there was me to consider! Word would spread that Huck Finn had helped a Black man gain his freedom. If I ever met anyone from that town again, I'd be ready to crawl down and lick his boots out of shame. That's how it goes: someone does something disgraceful, then doesn't want to face the consequences. He thinks there's no shame in it so long as he can keep it hidden. That was exactly my situation. The more I considered it, the harder my conscience worked on me, and the more wicked, mean, and rotten I felt.
